newsitem.title: USA: U.S. new home sales strong in Dec, '97 seen weaker.
newsitem.headline: U.S. new home sales strong in Dec, '97 seen weaker.

text.p: U.S. single-family home sales largely maintained their strength in December, but economists spotted a few chinks in the housing market's armor.
The annualized rate of new homes sales fell 1.0 percent in December to 783,000 units, the Commerce Department said. That surpassed Wall Street economists' forecast of 745,000 units.
Sales for all of 1996 jumped 13.3 percent to 756,000 units, the highest level since 1978.
But relatively high interest rates and waning demand should slow home sales near term, economists said.
"In the first quarter there will be some moderation," said Asha Bangalore, an economist at Northern Trust.
Much of the unsatisfied demand for new homes has been met, so sales should stabilize or decline, Bangalore said.
Supply-side pressures should also help contain sales, she said. New-home inventories rose only slightly in December to a 5.2-month supply, well below the 5.9-percent level reported for October.
"If you look at the inventory of unsold homes, it's very encouraging," Bangalore said. "There is not a big accumulation here."
The recent backup in interest rates has made mortgages more expensive, which should help to brake the housing market as well, economists said.

"Rates have moved up recently in November and December, and I think that gets us off in the first quarter with a slow decline (in home sales)," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
More broadly, the December home sales data confirmed the strength of the late-1996 economy and added to the view that 1997 began on solid footing.
"This is a reinforcement that the structural stability of the economy is there," Kretzmer said.
While the data are unlikely to influence this week's Fed policy meeting, speedy economic growth fueled by continued strong housing would have an effect, he said.
The central bank will probably raise rates unless first-quarter growth "slows substantially, down into the 2.0 to 2.5 percent range," Kretzmer said.
